reason: The text emphasizes hierarchical relationships throughout. Jacob exercises patriarchal authority over his sons, making decisions that they obey (whether to send Benjamin, when to return to Egypt). Joseph is positioned as a powerful official subordinate only to Pharaoh, wielding authority over his brothers. The narrative depicts multiple levels of hierarchy (Pharaoh > Joseph > brothers) as natural and expected, with characters showing deference to those of higher status. Judah emerges as a leader among the brothers and addresses Joseph with formal respect ('my lord'). Age and birth order carry significance, and there is no questioning of the legitimacy of these hierarchical arrangements—they are presented as the normal structure of both family and state.
